title: Pull your ears
hook: nodding Moggallana is given remedies for drowsiness: from pulling your ears to walking

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suppavasa's meal, and your line, a gift that comes back. Today, what happens after a good meal, when you sit down to meditate and your head starts to drop.

The breath is slow, the room is warm, and then your chin dips toward your chest, and you jerk back up, hoping no one saw. Anyone who has sat to meditate knows that moment. In the Book of Sevens, it happens to Moggallana, one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, famous in the tradition for his powers of mind. He's sitting in meditation near a village in Magadha, and he keeps nodding. The Buddha, the text says, sees it from far away, and comes to him with a list of remedies.
screen: `THE CHIN DIPS.` → `EVEN MOGGALLANA NODDED.` → `A LIST OF REMEDIES.`

segments.voice: Are you nodding, Moggallana? Yes, sir. Then comes a ladder, each step tried only if the one before doesn't work. First: whatever thought you were on when drowsiness came, stop giving it attention. Second: think over a teaching you've learned. Third: recite a teaching out loud, in detail. Fourth: pull both your earlobes and rub your limbs with your hands. Fifth: get up, wash your eyes with water, and look around in every direction, and up at the stars. Sixth: bring to mind the perception of light, the idea of daytime, day and night alike. Seventh: walk up and down, with your senses gathered in. And if none of that works? Eighth: lie down on your right side, like a lion, mindful, with the thought of getting up again, and when you wake, get up promptly. No one is scolded. Sleepiness isn't treated as a sin, just a state with causes and cures. Thinking, then talking, then the body, then cold water and open sky, then movement, and last of all, permission to rest. The order matters. The sutta goes on with advice on pride and on argument, but the ear-pulling is the part people remember.
screen: `ARE YOU NODDING, MOGGALLANA?` · `THINK, RECITE, PULL YOUR EARS.` · `WATER, STARS, LIGHT, WALKING.` · then, large: `LAST OF ALL, REST.`

segments.voice: Check your alertness right now, honestly. If it's low, try the fourth step: take both earlobes between thumb and finger and give them a slow pull, then rub your hands together and along your arms. If you're already alert, rest with the breath and learn what alertness feels like, so you'll know it when it fades.

pacala. The Pali word for nodding or drowsiness, the state of Moggallana in the Book of Sevens, met by the Buddha with a ladder of remedies from changing the thought to looking at the stars. Today's word.
Your line: climb the ladder. Rest is a rung too; it's just the last one. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions still give these remedies for sleepiness, such as opening the eyes, standing, or switching to walking meditation, and some retreats offer standing or walking periods for exactly this.

original.note: Pali pacala: nodding, drowsiness; the sutta's name, 'the nodding discourse.'

chat.says: I keep nodding off when I meditate. Did the Buddha say anything about that?
options: Yes: he gave Moggallana a ladder of remedies, from pulling your ears to walking, and last, rest.
Yes: he scolded Moggallana, saying sleepiness in meditation is a sin to confess.
No; he told Moggallana that nodding off means a person isn't suited to meditation.
chat.meaning: In AN 7.58 the Buddha gives nodding Moggallana remedies in order: change the thought, recite, pull your ears, water, stars, walking, and last, mindful rest.

Moggallana.meaning: one of the Buddha's two chief disciples

Magadha.meaning: a kingdom in the Buddha's India

Book of Sevens.meaning: the part of the Numbered Discourses grouped in sevens
